extracted.intended_audience: general readers, improvisational comedy enthusiasts and performers (esp. ComedySportz participants and organizers)
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of ComedySportz match format, scoring, referee role, and penalties (fouls) that govern performance content and conduct. Includes organizational notes about licensing, touring, and youth leagues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match format
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional format of a ComedySportz match features two teams of improvisational performers ("Players"), competing in various rounds, using improv games and performing scenes. Audience members judge the results and award points as directed by the Referee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matches consist of rounds and improv games; the flavor is compared to the television show Whose Line Is It Anyway? but is described as a more competitive and For Everyone (content-wise) version of Theatresports. Teams are often dynamic with rosters depending on which players are available, and match outcomes are not pre-determined as audience voting/selected judges decide the winner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee role
rubrics_metrics.description: In every match, a ComedySportz referee monitors the action, awarding points, and administering Fouls as necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The referee enforces rules, maintains flow, applies penalties for content or conduct infractions, and may exercise discretion to keep the match moving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience judging / scoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members judge the results and award points as directed by the Referee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match winners are chosen by audience voting or selected judges; scoring is audience-focused and part of the competitive framing of the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Out of Bounds Foul
rubrics_metrics.description: Called when a player uses explicit language or refers to something crass or off-color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Out of Bounds Foul is called, the offending player or audience member must spend the remainder of the game outside the theater space. They may or may not be welcomed back in. (Originally called the "Brown Bag Foul"—the bag was removed/replaced due to COVID-19 in 2022.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Groaner Foul
rubrics_metrics.description: Any player who speaks a pun bad enough to make the audience groan causing their team to lose one point (or awarding the other team with a point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The penalty can be negated if the player's apology to the audience is heartfelt enough and accepted. Example on page: "Why does the Norwegian navy put barcodes on ships? So they can Scandenavian."

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneously generated Fouls (referee discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any spontaneously generated Foul the referee feels is needed to move the match forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees have latitude to create/declare fouls in the moment to maintain pacing, audience engagement, or correct course during a match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content standard — "For Everyone" / clean content
rubrics_metrics.description: The CSz format is a more competitive and For Everyone (content-wise) version of Theatresports; penalties are put in place for the audience's benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on clean, audience-focused material (avoid explicit/off-color language) enables ComedySportz groups to perform road shows for corporate, college, church, school, and association clients and to run corporate team-building workshops. The same clean/content-appropriate standard applies when coaching or running high school and middle school leagues, where students perform shows similar to the professional level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team composition and dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the image of competition is maintained, the teams are often dynamic, with rosters depending on which player (many of whom have other occupations) are available for a match at any given time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers should expect variable rosters and plan matches accordingly; performances and judging remain live and audience-driven rather than pre-scripted.
